requested.title: /_heapsnapshot serves a full V8 heap dump (including MOCHI_KEY) to any unauthenticated client
/mcp retains attacker-chosen state forever with no auth, rate limit, or eviction
Draft blog posts are publicly readable because the deployed site runs NODE_ENV=development
/_profiler/start and /_profiler/stop are unauthenticated and deliberately not mode-gated
CSRF Origin enforcement is warn-only on the deployed site: proxy.origin is configured but never enforced
Server stack traces are rendered to clients on 5xx because the deployed site runs in development mode
Production release stage built on an unpinned third-party `:latest` base image

The two captcha routes 80 lines above do carry `{ rateLimit: ... }`, confirming the asymmetry. The site's `protection.protect` only matches `/demos/protection*`, so the PoW gate never covers /mcp, and CSRF is inapplicable because the transport demands `Content-Type: application/json` (and a non-browser attacker ignores it anyway). (2) Session retention: in `@tmcp/transport-http@0.8.6` `respond()`, `session_id = request.headers.get('mcp-session-id') || this.#options.getSessionId()` — client-supplied, unvalidated, unbounded. The constructor registers `#server.on('initialize', ...)` which calls `sessionManager.info.setClientCapabilities(sessionId, capabilities)` and `setClientInfo(...)`. The default `InMemoryInfoSessionManager` (`@tmcp/session-manager`) backs these with plain `Map`s — no size cap, no TTL, pruned only by `delete(id)`, reachable solely via an explicit DELETE for that exact id. In tmcp, `InitializeRequestParamsSchema.capabilities` is `ClientCapabilitiesSchema = v.looseObject({...})`, and valibot's `looseObject` preserves unknown keys verbatim, so an arbitrarily large/nested `params.capabilities` is retained as-is; `ImplementationSchema`'s `name`/`version` are unbounded `v.string()`. Mochi sets no `maxRequestBodySize`, so Bun's 128 MB default applies.     "findingId": "F5",
    "verdict": "true-positive",
    "adjustedSeverity": "MEDIUM",
    "reasoning": "Confirmed by tracing the whole path. Same root cause as F6 but a different control and a different downstream module, so I am keeping it separate rather than marking it duplicate: the impacts are distinct security classes (CWE-352 vs CWE-209), they live in different framework files (runtime/csrf.ts vs runtime/errors.ts), and each admits its own independent fix. Second, the finding's contrast that \"`packages/demos/src/index.ts:20` passes `development:` explicitly; this entry does not\" is a non-distinction: demos passes `development: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development'`, the identical expression, so it is equally inert. Neither caveat changes the verdict — a security control the config advertises is silently off in production, and any future authenticated action on this host inherits the hole."
  },
  {
    "findingId": "F3",
    "verdict": "true-positive",
    "reasoning": "The broken control is real and verified. routes.ts:89 defines `const DEVELOPMENT = process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development'`; line 229 calls `loadPosts({ includeDrafts: DEVELOPMENT })` and maps every returned post into props including `draft`; line 241 calls `getPost(slug, { includeDrafts: DEVELOPMENT })`. blog.ts:102-116 shows those options are the only thing hiding a draft — `loadPosts` filters on `!p.draft` unless `includeDrafts`, and `getPost` returns `null` for a draft unless `includeDrafts`. And `DEVELOPMENT` is true in the deployed container: the root Dockerfile's ENTRYPOINT is `bun run dev:${WORKSPACE}`, packages/site's `dev` script is `NODE_ENV=development bun src/index.ts`, build.yml's site leg builds from that Dockerfile, its matrix comment says \"Deployed in dev mode … so the debug toolbar and dev overlays are visible\", and lib/debugBarEncode.ts:1 opens with \"This site runs in dev mode in production\". The finding's strongest argument also checks out: every other surface hides drafts unconditionally — `buildSitemapXml` (docs.ts:300) and `buildFeedXml` call `loadPosts()` with no options, and `getPostLlmsTxt` (docs.ts:330) calls `getPost(slug)` with no options, so `/blog//llms.txt` would 404 for a post whose HTML page serves fine. That asymmetry is strong evidence `includeDrafts: DEVELOPMENT` was written to mean \"local only\", which this deployment is not. The recommendation's pointer to og/resolve.ts:34 is also correct — it repeats the same `getPost(postSlug, { includeDrafts: DEVELOPMENT })` pattern. One material scoping fact the finding omits: there are currently no drafts. `ls packages/site/src/blog/` returns four posts and `grep '^draft:'` across them returns nothing, so nothing is being disclosed right now. The exposure is latent: the moment a `draft: true` post is committed — the exact case the flag exists for, e.g. an embargoed release announcement staged ahead of a launch — it is listed on /blog/ and readable at /blog// with no gate. I am leaving severity at MEDIUM: the control failure is unconditional and the content class (pre-publication announcements on a release-blogging site) is a genuine if modest confidentiality concern, even though today's concrete impact is zero."
  },
  {
    "findingId": "F7",
    "verdict": "true-positive",
    "adjustedSeverity": "BUG",
    "reasoning": "The central factual claim is accurate and verified: packages/demos/Dockerfile.production:30 is `FROM frolvlad/alpine-glibc:latest AS release` — a mutable tag on a non-official third-party Docker Hub account, with no version floor and no digest, in the stage that becomes the runtime filesystem. Every rebuild resolves `:latest` to whatever that account currently publishes, and line 57's `apk add --no-cache libgcc ncdu` inherits whatever repository snapshot that image pins. It is genuinely the repo's outlier: I checked every Dockerfile and all the others pin a specific official tag — root `Dockerfile`, `Dockerfile.production` and `Dockerfile.memtest` all use `ARG BUN_IMAGE=oven/bun:1.4.4-alpine`, `packages/minimal/Dockerfile` uses `oven/bun:1.4.4-alpine`, `.devcontainer/Dockerfile` uses `node:24-slim`, and this file's own base stage uses `oven/bun:1.4.4`. The repo has already moved away from this base elsewhere for unrelated reasons — root Dockerfile:14-17 notes \"Earlier revisions used frolvlad/alpine-glibc with a copied bun binary; that combo broke @tailwindcss/oxide's native binding on linux/arm64\" — so this is a stale leftover. The finding's reachability hedge is also correct: build.yml's demos matrix leg specifies `dockerfile: Dockerfile`, not this file, so it is not on the CI/CapRover deploy route and is only built by hand. I am downgrading from MEDIUM to BUG for two reasons. First, there is no remotely triggerable attack — exploitation is wholly contingent on an upstream account or pipeline compromise, and the artifact is not deployed, so this is dependency hygiene rather than an exposure. Second, the two secondary claims do not hold up as outliers: the root Dockerfile also runs `apk add --no-cache ncdu` and also does `chown -R bun:bun packages/${WORKSPACE}/src`, with an in-file rationale (\"demos' tailwind step writes app.generated.css into src/ at startup\"), so both are the repo's deliberate, documented, repo-wide pattern and not something this file introduces. The pinning recommendation is still worth taking."
  },
  {
    "findingId": "F1",
    "verdict": "false-positive",
    "reasoning": "The technical description of the route is accurate — routes.ts:156-172 registers `/_heapsnapshot` as a bare `Mochi.api()` with no auth, no `rateLimit`, no `DEVELOPMENT` guard and no client-address check, and it does `Bun.gc(true)` then returns `Bun.generateHeapSnapshot('v8')` verbatim, which in V8 format includes a string table and would therefore carry `process.env` values such as MOCHI_KEY. But the finding is not exploitable against anything that runs, and the gap is reachability, not route-level defense. I traced every place the flag can be set: `grep -rn HEAP_SNAPSHOTS_ENABLED` across the repo returns only routes.ts itself, memtest/driver.ts comments, memtest/README.md, and `Dockerfile.memtest:55`. It appears in no `.env` file (I checked `.env`, `.env.example`, `packages/demos/.env`, `packages/support/.env*`), no compose file, and nowhere in `.github/workflows/build.yml` — whose three legs build site and demos from the root `Dockerfile` and support from `Dockerfile.production`, neither of which sets it. So on every CI-built, CapRover-deployed image the route is simply not registered; `routes` never contains the key. In the one image that does set it, exposure is blocked a second time: `memtest/run.sh` leaves `PUBLISH` empty by default and its `docker run` therefore passes no `-p`, so the container's `EXPOSE ${PORT}/tcp` publishes nothing (EXPOSE is metadata only without `-p`/`-P`), and `memtest/driver.ts` reaches the site over `127.0.0.1` inside the container. The continuous harness does not change this — `memtest/loop.sh:86` invokes `bash memtest/run.sh` without setting `PUBLISH`. The repo also documents this exact threat rather than overlooking it: run.sh's comment says \"publishing would expose /_heapsnapshot (a full heap dump) … to the network. Set PUBLISH to a host address to map it anyway — PUBLISH=127.0.0.1 for local-only access\", the README repeats it, and routes.ts:153-155 says the route \"stays unregistered unless explicitly opted into\". Constructing an attack requires positing an operator either setting an env var no deploy artifact sets, or publishing a port the harness deliberately withholds against its own written advice — that is operator misconfiguration of debug tooling, not a vulnerability in the shipped artifact. I do want to preserve the signal: the recommendation is sound and cheap (the driver talks to loopback, so a `getClientAddress()` loopback check costs the only caller nothing), and it would convert two deployment conventions into one in-code invariant. Worth doing as hardening; not a live finding."
  },
  {
    "findingId": "F4",
    "verdict": "false-positive",
    "reasoning": "Every statement about the route shape is correct, and I confirmed the profiler internals: lib/profiler.ts gates on `process.env.MOCHI_PROFILER === '1'`, `startProfiler()` attaches a `node:inspector/promises` Session and posts `Profiler.enable`/`Profiler.start` with no auto-stop, `stopProfiler()` throws `new Error('profiler not started')` when no session exists (surfacing as a 500 through the api route's error path), and routes.ts:141-152 wraps both in bare `Mochi.api()` handlers with no auth and no rate limit. The comment at line 140 does deliberately remove mode gating. None of that is exploitable, though, because the flag is never set anywhere a request can reach. `grep -rn MOCHI_PROFILER` across the repo returns exactly three hits: lib/profiler.ts:5, and scripts/flamegraph.ts:155/158. flamegraph.ts is a developer-local script that *spawns its own site process* (`spawn({ cmd: ['bun', 'src/index.ts'], cwd: packages/site, env: { ...process.env, PORT, MOCHI_PROFILER: '1' } })` with `delete env.NODE_ENV`) and then talks to it at `http://localhost:${args.port}` — so the flagged process is a short-lived child of the developer's own terminal, not a served deployment. The flag appears in no Dockerfile (I read all six), no `.env` file, no compose file, and nowhere in build.yml. The finding's inference that \"`scripts/flamegraph.ts:155` sets `MOCHI_PROFILER=1` against a *production-mode* site, confirming the flag is expected to travel with production builds\" conflates two different things: `delete env.NODE_ENV` makes the child run in production *mode*, which is why the mode guard was removed, but that child is still a local process on localhost — it says nothing about the flag travelling into a deployed image, and nothing in the repo carries it there. Structurally identical to F1: the env-var gate means the routes do not exist on any internet-facing process, so I cannot describe a concrete attack without positing an operator setting a flag no deploy artifact sets. As with F1, the hardening is still worth taking — flamegraph.ts spawns the server locally, so binding these to loopback via `getClientAddress()` costs the only caller nothing, and an auto-stop timeout would close the forgotten-`start` case."
  }
]

**Summary of what changed from the submitted findings:**

| ID | Verdict | Note |
|---|---|---|
| F1 | **false-positive** | `HEAP_SNAPSHOTS_ENABLED` is set only in `Dockerfile.memtest`, which isn't in build.yml's matrix; `run.sh`/`loop.sh` never publish the port. Route unregistered on every deployed image. Hardening still advisable. |
| F2 | **true-positive** (MEDIUM) | Confirmed in all three parts, including the `looseObject` capability retention and the miss-caching at `docs.ts:208`. tmcp has no init-order gate, so `tools/call` needs no handshake. |
| F3 | **true-positive** | Control verifiably broken; impact is latent — there are currently zero `draft: true` posts. |
| F4 | **false-positive** | `MOCHI_PROFILER=1` is set only by `scripts/flamegraph.ts`, which spawns its own local child and talks to localhost. The "production build" in that comment is a local process, not a deployment. |
| F5 | **true-positive** | Origin check verifiably inert. Kept separate from F6. Two corrections: the login cookie's `SameSite=Lax` blunts the authenticated case, and the `packages/demos` contrast is a non-distinction (identical expression). |
| F6 | **true-positive** | Worse than reported — `error(404)` throws `MochiHttpError extends Error`, so *any* page 404 renders a stack, not just 5xx. But the `debugBarEncode.ts` supporting argument is a misread: its motive is SEO, and it decodes losslessly, so paths are already public. |
| F7 | **true-positive** → **BUG** | `:latest` claim verified and it is the repo's only outlier. Downgraded: not on the deploy route, no remote trigger. The `ncdu`/`chown src` sub-claims aren't outliers — the root Dockerfile does both, deliberately. |

And `DEVELOPMENT` is true in the deployed container: the root Dockerfile's ENTRYPOINT is `bun run dev:${WORKSPACE}`, packages/site's `dev` script is `NODE_ENV=development bun src/index.ts`, build.yml's site leg builds from that Dockerfile, its matrix comment says "Deployed in dev mode … so the debug toolbar and dev overlays are visible", and lib/debugBarEncode.ts:1 opens with "This site runs in dev mode in production". The finding's strongest argument also checks out: every other surface hides drafts unconditionally — `buildSitemapXml` (docs.ts:300) and `buildFeedXml` call `loadPosts()` with no options, and `getPostLlmsTxt` (docs.ts:330) calls `getPost(slug)` with no options, so `/blog/<slug>/llms.txt` would 404 for a post whose HTML page serves fine. That asymmetry is strong evidence `includeDrafts: DEVELOPMENT` was written to mean "local only", which this deployment is not. The recommendation's pointer to og/resolve.ts:34 is also correct — it repeats the same `getPost(postSlug, { includeDrafts: DEVELOPMENT })` pattern. One material scoping fact the finding omits: there are currently no drafts. `ls packages/site/src/blog/` returns four posts and `grep '^draft:'` across them returns nothing, so nothing is being disclosed right now. The exposure is latent: the moment a `draft: true` post is committed — the exact case the flag exists for, e.g. an embargoed release announcement staged ahead of a launch — it is listed on /blog/ and readable at /blog/<slug>/ with no gate. I am leaving severity at MEDIUM: the control failure is unconditional and the content class (pre-publication announcements on a release-blogging site) is a genuine if modest confidentiality concern, even though today's concrete impact is zero.

The central factual claim is accurate and verified: packages/demos/Dockerfile.production:30 is `FROM frolvlad/alpine-glibc:latest AS release` — a mutable tag on a non-official third-party Docker Hub account, with no version floor and no digest, in the stage that becomes the runtime filesystem. Every rebuild resolves `:latest` to whatever that account currently publishes, and line 57's `apk add --no-cache libgcc ncdu` inherits whatever repository snapshot that image pins. It is genuinely the repo's outlier: I checked every Dockerfile and all the others pin a specific official tag — root `Dockerfile`, `Dockerfile.production` and `Dockerfile.memtest` all use `ARG BUN_IMAGE=oven/bun:1.4.4-alpine`, `packages/minimal/Dockerfile` uses `oven/bun:1.4.4-alpine`, `.devcontainer/Dockerfile` uses `node:24-slim`, and this file's own base stage uses `oven/bun:1.4.4`. The repo has already moved away from this base elsewhere for unrelated reasons — root Dockerfile:14-17 notes "Earlier revisions used frolvlad/alpine-glibc with a copied bun binary; that combo broke @tailwindcss/oxide's native binding on linux/arm64" — so this is a stale leftover. The finding's reachability hedge is also correct: build.yml's demos matrix leg specifies `dockerfile: Dockerfile`, not this file, so it is not on the CI/CapRover deploy route and is only built by hand. I am downgrading from MEDIUM to BUG for two reasons. First, there is no remotely triggerable attack — exploitation is wholly contingent on an upstream account or pipeline compromise, and the artifact is not deployed, so this is dependency hygiene rather than an exposure. Second, the two secondary claims do not hold up as outliers: the root Dockerfile also runs `apk add --no-cache ncdu` and also does `chown -R bun:bun packages/${WORKSPACE}/src`, with an in-file rationale ("demos' tailwind step writes app.generated.css into src/ at startup"), so both are the repo's deliberate, documented, repo-wide pattern and not something this file introduces. The pinning recommendation is still worth taking.

The technical description of the route is accurate — routes.ts:156-172 registers `/_heapsnapshot` as a bare `Mochi.api()` with no auth, no `rateLimit`, no `DEVELOPMENT` guard and no client-address check, and it does `Bun.gc(true)` then returns `Bun.generateHeapSnapshot('v8')` verbatim, which in V8 format includes a string table and would therefore carry `process.env` values such as MOCHI_KEY. But the finding is not exploitable against anything that runs, and the gap is reachability, not route-level defense. I traced every place the flag can be set: `grep -rn HEAP_SNAPSHOTS_ENABLED` across the repo returns only routes.ts itself, memtest/driver.ts comments, memtest/README.md, and `Dockerfile.memtest:55`. It appears in no `.env` file (I checked `.env`, `.env.example`, `packages/demos/.env`, `packages/support/.env*`), no compose file, and nowhere in `.github/workflows/build.yml` — whose three legs build site and demos from the root `Dockerfile` and support from `Dockerfile.production`, neither of which sets it. So on every CI-built, CapRover-deployed image the route is simply not registered; `routes` never contains the key. In the one image that does set it, exposure is blocked a second time: `memtest/run.sh` leaves `PUBLISH` empty by default and its `docker run` therefore passes no `-p`, so the container's `EXPOSE ${PORT}/tcp` publishes nothing (EXPOSE is metadata only without `-p`/`-P`), and `memtest/driver.ts` reaches the site over `127.0.0.1` inside the container. The continuous harness does not change this — `memtest/loop.sh:86` invokes `bash memtest/run.sh` without setting `PUBLISH`. The repo also documents this exact threat rather than overlooking it: run.sh's comment says "publishing would expose /_heapsnapshot (a full heap dump) … to the network. Set PUBLISH to a host address to map it anyway — PUBLISH=127.0.0.1 for local-only access", the README repeats it, and routes.ts:153-155 says the route "stays unregistered unless explicitly opted into". Constructing an attack requires positing an operator either setting an env var no deploy artifact sets, or publishing a port the harness deliberately withholds against its own written advice — that is operator misconfiguration of debug tooling, not a vulnerability in the shipped artifact. I do want to preserve the signal: the recommendation is sound and cheap (the driver talks to loopback, so a `getClientAddress()` loopback check costs the only caller nothing), and it would convert two deployment conventions into one in-code invariant. Worth doing as hardening; not a live finding.

Every statement about the route shape is correct, and I confirmed the profiler internals: lib/profiler.ts gates on `process.env.MOCHI_PROFILER === '1'`, `startProfiler()` attaches a `node:inspector/promises` Session and posts `Profiler.enable`/`Profiler.start` with no auto-stop, `stopProfiler()` throws `new Error('profiler not started')` when no session exists (surfacing as a 500 through the api route's error path), and routes.ts:141-152 wraps both in bare `Mochi.api()` handlers with no auth and no rate limit. The comment at line 140 does deliberately remove mode gating. None of that is exploitable, though, because the flag is never set anywhere a request can reach. `grep -rn MOCHI_PROFILER` across the repo returns exactly three hits: lib/profiler.ts:5, and scripts/flamegraph.ts:155/158. flamegraph.ts is a developer-local script that *spawns its own site process* (`spawn({ cmd: ['bun', 'src/index.ts'], cwd: packages/site, env: { ...process.env, PORT, MOCHI_PROFILER: '1' } })` with `delete env.NODE_ENV`) and then talks to it at `http://localhost:${args.port}` — so the flagged process is a short-lived child of the developer's own terminal, not a served deployment. The flag appears in no Dockerfile (I read all six), no `.env` file, no compose file, and nowhere in build.yml. The finding's inference that "`scripts/flamegraph.ts:155` sets `MOCHI_PROFILER=1` against a *production-mode* site, confirming the flag is expected to travel with production builds" conflates two different things: `delete env.NODE_ENV` makes the child run in production *mode*, which is why the mode guard was removed, but that child is still a local process on localhost — it says nothing about the flag travelling into a deployed image, and nothing in the repo carries it there. Structurally identical to F1: the env-var gate means the routes do not exist on any internet-facing process, so I cannot describe a concrete attack without positing an operator setting a flag no deploy artifact sets. As with F1, the hardening is still worth taking — flamegraph.ts spawns the server locally, so binding these to loopback via `getClientAddress()` costs the only caller nothing, and an auto-stop timeout would close the forgotten-`start` case.
